title: React Components, JSX, Props, and State
description: Learn to describe UI declaratively, compose reusable function components, pass read-only props, and update state with useState.
learningOutcomes: Create function components and compose them into a page.
Read JSX expressions and conditionally render elements.
Pass data with props and treat props as read-only.
Use useState for values that change over time and should update the UI.
Update arrays and objects immutably and use functional state updates when appropriate.

blocks.text: React describes the UI for the current state

In imperative DOM code, an event handler often finds an element and changes its text or classes directly. React uses a declarative model: components describe the interface for the current props and state, and React reconciles that description with the DOM. Rather than manually patching the same DOM nodes, update the data that drives the UI and let React render the result.

blocks.title: A component is a reusable UI unit
blocks.text: A function component receives props, can read its own state, and returns React elements. React may call it again when its inputs change. Rendering should describe the UI, while event handlers request state changes in response to user interactions.

A function component has a name that starts with an uppercase letter and returns React elements. JSX lets you describe the element tree using markup-like syntax that the build tool transforms into JavaScript. Use curly braces to evaluate JavaScript expressions, className for CSS classes, and a parent element or Fragment when you need to return multiple siblings.

steps.title: Describe the markup with JSX
steps.explanation: JSX describes a section and its children. Curly braces evaluate the name expression, while className supplies a CSS class.

items: Use {expression} to insert a JavaScript expression into JSX; arbitrary statements such as if cannot be placed directly in an expression slot.
Use condition ? <A /> : <B /> or ordinary if logic before return for conditional rendering.
Use map to render a collection and give each sibling a stable key.
Component names start with an uppercase letter; native HTML tags are lowercase.
Props are data or callbacks supplied by the parent and are not a place to mutate parent-owned values.

blocks.text: Props let a parent pass strings, numbers, booleans, objects, arrays, and callbacks to a child. Treat these values as read-only. If a child needs to ask for a change, it can invoke a callback supplied by the parent or manage appropriate local state. A component should render from current props, not assume the values never change.

blocks.caption: Pass data and behavior into a reusable card

blocks.text: A local variable inside a component function is recreated when React calls that function again. Changing such a variable does not notify React that the UI needs an update. useState gives React a value to retain between renders and a setter that schedules an update. The state value observed by the currently executing render is a snapshot; calling the setter does not change that snapshot in place.

steps.title: Initialize the state value
steps.explanation: useState(0) uses zero for the first render and returns the current value plus a setter.

steps.title: Display the current snapshot
steps.explanation: The count expression is evaluated for this render. After a state update, React calls the component again with the new state value.

steps.title: Request an update from an event
steps.explanation: The setter schedules a state update. React coordinates the next render and DOM changes; this is not a direct DOM mutation.

blocks.text: When state contains an array or object, return a new array or object to represent a change. Methods such as map, filter, and object spread help express the update while preserving unrelated items or properties. If the next state depends on the pending previous state—especially for multiple queued increments—use the functional updater form so each updater receives the latest queued value.

steps.title: Queue state updates based on pending state
steps.explanation: Every updater receives the pending value produced by the previous updater. This reliably adds three even though all calls occur in one handler.

steps.title: Represent object changes with a new value
steps.explanation: Spread copies the top-level properties into a new object and then overrides role. The existing name is retained.

blocks.title: Follow the Rules of Hooks
blocks.text: Call useState and other Hooks at the top level of a function component or custom Hook, not inside loops, conditions, or nested functions. A consistent call order lets React associate each Hook with the correct state/effect between renders.

blocks.prompt: What happens when a useState setter receives a different next value?

options.text: React schedules an update and renders again when appropriate
options.feedback: The setter informs React about changed state; React updates the rendered UI according to the new value.

options.text: It directly edits the DOM node containing the value
options.feedback: React coordinates DOM updates from rendered output; the setter is not a direct DOM API.
A local state update normally causes a React render, not a full-page reload.

options.text: The state variable changes immediately in the currently executing render
options.feedback: The current render keeps its snapshot; the new value is used in a subsequent render.

blocks.explanation: State setters schedule state updates; the current render's captured state value remains a snapshot.

blocks.prompt: A child should mutate an object prop when the user clicks a button.

options.feedback: Mutating a prop bypasses the intended owner-controlled data flow and may not trigger a React render.
Props are read-only inputs; use a callback or appropriate local state to request a change.

blocks.explanation: Props provide one-way data flow from parent to child.

blocks.prompt: Which practices follow common React state guidance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use a functional updater when the next value depends on prior state
options.feedback: Updater functions receive the pending previous value and compose correctly when updates are queued.

options.text: Create a new array or object when updating structured state
options.feedback: Immutable updates make transitions explicit and preserve predictable references.

options.text: Call useState conditionally inside an if statement
options.feedback: Hooks must be called in the same order at the top level on every render.

options.text: Mutate the state object and pass the same reference back
options.feedback: In-place mutation hides the change and can cause React to treat the value as unchanged.

blocks.explanation: Use predictable immutable updates and follow the Rules of Hooks.

blocks.title: Build a counter and a task list with React state
blocks.context: Implement this in a React project. The lesson editor stores the draft but does not compile TSX in the browser.
instructions: Create a Counter component using useState and an increment button.
Add a button that increments the counter by three with functional updaters.
Define a Task type with id, title, and completed.
Render tasks from state with stable keys and allow a task to be marked complete using map.
Add tasks by returning a new array rather than mutating the previous one.
Explain why changing a local variable does not cause a render while setting state does.
If extracting a TaskItem component, pass props and avoid mutating them.
Test repeated clicks and the addition of multiple tasks.
requirements: Component functions return valid JSX and use PascalCase naming.
The count value comes from useState, not a mutable local variable.
Increment by three uses functional updates.
Task additions and completion updates are immutable.
The learner can explain props, state snapshots, and re-rendering.
hints: Return a new array from every task update rather than mutating the existing array.
Use map to preserve each task and change only the one with the matching ID.
Use updater functions for multiple increments that depend on the prior count.
successCriteria: The count responds to every click.
The increment-by-three control adds exactly three.
Adding tasks preserves previous task data.
Completing one task leaves other tasks unchanged.
Every list item has a stable key.
You can explain why React state differs from a local variable.

items: Components describe the UI declaratively from props and state.
JSX describes elements and uses braces for JavaScript expressions.
Props are read-only inputs; state represents values that change over time.
useState setters schedule rendering; they do not directly mutate the DOM or current render snapshot.
Update arrays and objects immutably, and use functional updaters when the next value depends on previous state.

blocks.text: Deep dive: state snapshots, queued updates, and immutable objects

A render observes a snapshot of state. Calling a setter schedules a future render; it does not mutate the state variable inside the currently running event handler. When the next value depends on the previous one, use the functional updater form. For objects and arrays, return a new reference instead of mutating the previous snapshot.

steps.title: The handler captures the current render snapshot
steps.explanation: If count is 0, all three `count + 1` expressions read 0 and request the value 1. These calls do not read a freshly mutated local variable after each setter.

steps.title: Functional updaters are processed in the queue
steps.explanation: Each updater receives the result of the preceding queued update, so the three increments produce an increase of three.

steps.title: Keep state updates immutable
steps.explanation: The button renders the current snapshot and calls the event handler when clicked. For nested objects, copy the object levels you change so React receives a new reference.

items: Use `setCount(n => n + 1)` when the next state depends on the previous state, especially for multiple queued updates.
Treat state values as read-only snapshots. Do not call `push`, mutate an object in place, or rely on assigning to a local variable to trigger render.
Store the minimum source of truth. Derive filtered lists, totals and display labels during render unless measuring shows a computation is genuinely expensive.
Controlled inputs render their value from React state; update the state in `onChange`. Use a suitable initial value to avoid switching between uncontrolled and controlled modes.
Props are inputs from a parent, not a second copy of local state by default. If a value must remain shared, decide explicitly where its owner lives.

blocks.prompt: If count is 0 when `addThree()` runs, what value do three calls to `setCount(count + 1)` typically request in the same handler?

options.text: 3, because each setter updates count immediately
options.feedback: The local count variable is the snapshot from the current render and is not changed immediately by calling a setter.

options.text: 1, because each expression reads the same render snapshot
options.feedback: Each `count + 1` is evaluated against the same snapshot. Functional updaters are used when each queued update should build on the previous queued result.
Batching does not make the state undefined; it schedules updates so React can process them together.

options.text: The code always throws a runtime error
options.feedback: This code is valid. Its surprising behavior comes from state snapshots, not a runtime exception.

blocks.explanation: A setter schedules a state update; it does not rewrite the variable captured by the current handler.

blocks.title: Fix a stale state update and immutable profile editor
blocks.context: Use this task in a React project because the lesson playground does not compile TSX.
instructions: Implement a button that increments a counter three times in one event.
Use functional updater callbacks to make the three increments accumulate.
Implement a profile update that changes one nested field without mutating the original state.
Explain why the handler reads a snapshot and why a derived total need not be stored in state.
Initialize controlled inputs with a defined value and update them from onChange.
requirements: One click increases the count by three.
Previous state is read through the updater callback for dependent updates.
Object updates preserve untouched fields and create new references along the changed path.
Derived values are computed from source state rather than synchronized redundantly.
Controlled input values do not switch between undefined and defined unexpectedly.
hints: The current handler sees the state values from the render that created it.
Use the callback form of the setter when calculating a new value from an old one.
Copy every nested object on the path to a property you change.
successCriteria: One click increases count by exactly three.
The updater is based on previous state.
The original user/profile object is unchanged.
Derived state and controlled input ownership are explained.

items: React state is read as a render snapshot; setters schedule future work.
Functional updaters compose when next state depends on previous state.
Immutability and one clear owner for each piece of state simplify rendering and debugging.
